rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If “scriptures of Abraham” denotes texts preserving his teachings, the attribution remains correct even if later exegesis appears in them.
rows.anchor: if by the scriptures of Abraham (sws) the reference is to the ones in which his teachings are mentioned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rule that no soul bears another’s burden is taught in Moses’ and Abraham’s scriptures and refutes baseless intercession, the sūrah’s subject.
rows.anchor: This in fact is a refutation of the baseless concept of intercession which is the subject of this sūrah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Torah and Injil repeatedly teach this rule, making it surprising that their recipients were led by Satan into polytheism.
rows.anchor: This teaching is mentioned in the Torah and the Injil at so many instances

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each person receives only what they strive for; a pious ancestor’s reward does not transfer to descendants.
rows.anchor: no soul will be rewarded for the virtues of another or punished for the misdeeds of someone else

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah’s son, Abraham’s father, and Lot’s wife could not benefit from their prophetic relatives, while Pharaoh’s wife is praised in 66:11.
rows.anchor: even the closest relations of a prophet whose record was devoid of good deeds were not able to benefit from this relationship

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person’s good deed benefiting another must rest on their affectionate relationship of faith.
rows.anchor: this good deed should be based on a person’s affectionate relationship of faith with another person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person also shares in another’s good deed through a direct or indirect role, such as teaching, serving as an example, or financial help.
rows.anchor: a believer taught a believer or became an exemplar of a teaching for the other person or had financially helped the other person

rows.speaker: Some people having a socialistic mentality
rows.claim: They read the verse as requiring earnings proportionate to labor; Islahi rejects this as unrelated to the context and a misuse of intelligence.
rows.anchor: that a person should earn what is commensurate to the work he put in

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worldly provision is distributed to test gratitude and patience, while the Hereafter settles matters through justice and earned reward.
rows.anchor: He has blessed some abundantly and some stringently and in this manner tested the gratefulness and patience of both.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who pass the worldly trial are rewarded for their deeds; those who fail receive no reward and go to Hell.
rows.anchor: people who pass this trial will be rewarded for their good deeds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise that a person’s work will be seen and repaid assures believers that even tiny good deeds count and warns that no small evil deed is ignored.
rows.anchor: the believers should rest assured that the smallest of their good deeds shall be taken notice of

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Everyone returns to God and cannot appeal to another being to escape accountability; God’s decisions are final.
rows.anchor: Everyone will be brought before God and all decisions of God will be final and irrevocable.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone creates the circumstances for joy and sorrow, so no other being can be Lord over people.
rows.anchor: it is only He Who creates the circumstances for joy and only He Who creates the circumstances for sorrow.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only God grants life and death, which rules out anyone else’s lordship.
rows.anchor: it is only in God’s authority to grant life and death.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God created both man and woman as counterparts; there are no separate creators assigning sons and daughters.
rows.anchor: It is God Who has created the counterparts of a pair: man and woman.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone knows and nurtures the drop’s development, including whether a child forms and what sex and appearance it will have; therefore people should seek children from Him.
rows.anchor: All these details are only known to the great creator Who has knowledge of all things and Who nurtures this fluid within multifarious layers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The God who creates each person from a drop can recreate them; resurrection is needed so divine justice and mercy can fully appear.
rows.anchor: the need for it to happen is also obvious so that God’s justice and mercy can completely manifest themselves

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s declaration says that God will bring him back to life after death, echoing the passage’s affirmation of resurrection.
rows.anchor: who will cause me to die and then bring me back to life; who, I hope, will forgive me my sins

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With slight variations, these divine acts echo Abraham’s declaration of acquittal against his people in 26:78–82.
rows.anchor: Who has created me; then he guides me

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God moves people from poverty to sufficiency and affluence; Islahi distinguishes the enrichment term from merely emerging from poverty by its sense of accumulated wealth.
rows.anchor: which is used for accumulated wealth. So the word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wealth of rich people who withhold spending while dreaming of Paradise comes from God, not Sirius, which God also rules.
rows.anchor: the character of those rich people is referred to who, though do not spend in the cause of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arab idolaters considered Sirius blessed and credited it with spring’s lushness and their trade activity.
rows.anchor: idolaters of Arabia regarded it to be very blessed and would attribute the lushness of spring as well as their own trade activities to it.

rows.speaker: A poet of the age of ignorance
rows.claim: The cited poem praises a man as warming people in cold winters and providing coolness and shade when Sirius appears.
rows.anchor: A poet of the age of ignorance while praising a praiseworthy person says:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah’s opening argument that stars set and fall reinforces that the stars people treat as fate-makers are themselves ruled by God.
rows.anchor: bear witness through their own setting and falling that only God is their Lord.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage adds extensions grounded in the original scriptural statement, a Qur’anic pattern that here turns the discourse from verse 40 onward into commentary on Quraysh.
rows.anchor: There are several examples in the Qur’ān in which a statement is cited and then certain additions are made in it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The extended discourse warns Quraysh that ʿĀd, Thamūd, and Noah’s people were warned, ignored their messengers, and were destroyed; Quraysh face the same fate if they follow them.
rows.anchor: were also warned by their respective messengers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ʿĀd here are the ancient or first ʿĀd; the Thamūd descended from them and were also called the second ʿĀd.
rows.anchor: descendents and were also known as the second

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their destruction was just punishment for their own injustice and rebellion; a nation’s internal causes emerge as disasters or enemy attacks.
rows.anchor: the real reasons for the destruction of a nation are not external; they arise from within it and take the form of earthquakes, floods and storms

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The overthrown cities in these verses refer to the people of Lot.
rows.anchor: This is a reference to the people of Lot.

rows.speaker: Lisān al-‘arab
rows.claim: The lexicon explains al-muʾtafikāt as winds that overturn a place like a harvester, and also uses it for a flood depositing mud and sand.
rows.anchor: those winds which totally turn a place topsy turvy the way a harvester turns a cultivated land topsy turvy.
